explanations.explanation: I see why that might sound right, but Jesus says the opposite. He tells them, “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans.” That's a closed door, not an open one. He sends them “…to the lost sheep of Israel.” instead.

You've got it, baker. Jesus says, “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans.” Samaritan towns are off the route for this trip. He points them to “…the lost sheep of Israel.” instead.

True, and it's right there in the list. Jesus says, “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, drive out demons.” That's four jobs, and none of them is small. I get nervous when I have to flip a whole tray without a crumb falling off.

It's actually true, and Jesus says it plainly. His words are, “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, drive out demons.” Raising the dead sits right in the middle of that list. Nobody could say they weren't told.
Freely is the word, friend. Jesus says, “Freely you have received; freely give.” They got it as a gift, so they hand it out the same way. No price tag, no fine print.
I get why careful sounds sensible, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says, “Freely you have received; freely give.” The way they received is the way they give. It's a gift going both directions.
Jesus doesn't say quietly. He says, “Freely you have received; freely give.” Remember He also tells them to preach as they go, so these twelve aren't sneaking around. The word is freely.
A second tunic is on the list. Jesus says, “Take no bag for the road, or second tunic, or sandals, or staff…” So no spare tunic goes along. I'd miss my spare apron already.

Nets are a fun guess, but they're not on Jesus' list. He says, “Take no bag for the road, or second tunic, or sandals, or staff…” The list also covers gold, silver and copper in their belts. A second tunic is the one on this card.

Scrolls never come up in this list. What Jesus names is gold, silver, copper, a bag, a second tunic, sandals and a staff. The second tunic is the answer here. Lots of things stay behind, but scrolls aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: A worker deserves to be provided for
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives. He says, “for the worker is worthy of his provisions.” So the twelve are workers, and they'll be provided for along the way. Packing light is the easy part when someone else is handling supplies.

explanations.answer: The towns are close to each other
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about how close the towns are. The reason He gives is, “for the worker is worthy of his provisions.” Provisions for the worker, that's the point. Distance doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: The trip will only take a day
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say how long the trip takes. Jesus gives one reason for traveling light: “for the worker is worthy of his provisions.” The workers get provided for. A schedule isn't mentioned.
Stay is the word. Jesus says to find out who is worthy and “…stay at his house until you move on.” One house, no hopping around. I like it, because I'd never leave a kitchen that smelled good.

Preaching is part of the trip, since Jesus tells them earlier to preach that the kingdom of heaven is near. But in this verse the instruction is to “…stay at his house until you move on.” The blank wants stay.

Praying is a fine thing to do, but it's not the instruction in this verse. Jesus says to find out who is worthy in that town and “…stay at his house until you move on.” The very next verse tells them what to do when they enter the home: greet its occupants. Praying never comes up in that stretch, so the blank wants stay.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, “If the home is worthy, let your peace rest on it, but if it is not, let your peace return to you.” So when the home is not worthy, the peace returns to the twelve. It doesn't stay on that home.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “If the home is worthy, let your peace rest on it, but if it is not, let your peace return to you.” An unworthy home means the peace comes back to the twelve. Nothing gets lost along the way.

explanations.answer: Shake the dust off their feet
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's what Jesus says. If anyone won't welcome them or heed their words, they should “…shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.” It's a clear sign as they walk away. Then they keep moving down the road.

explanations.answer: Sing a psalm at the gate
explanations.explanation: Singing is a lovely idea, but Jesus doesn't say it here. He says, “…shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.” The action is about their feet and the road. No gate and no song.

Jesus doesn't tell them to tear their robes or weep. His words are, “…shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.” That's the move for a home or town that won't welcome them. Dusty feet, then onward.

Sodom and Gomorrah are the two. Jesus says, “…it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.” This is a serious line, so I'll say it plainly. He is talking about a town that won't welcome the twelve.

Those two are big names in the Bible, but Jesus doesn't use them here. He says, “…it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.” It's a heavy comparison. Sodom and Gomorrah are the answer.

Jericho and Ai don't appear in this verse. Jesus names two other cities: “…it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.” It's a weighty line, so I'll say it plainly. Sodom and Gomorrah are the pair.

explanations.answer: Sharp and pure at the same time
explanations.explanation: That's the combination. Jesus says, “…be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.” Shrewd is the sharp part and innocent is the pure part, and He asks for both together. Not one or the other, both.
Jesus doesn't ask them to hide. He says, “…be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.” That's sharp and pure, together. Hiding isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: Bold and ready to fight back
explanations.explanation: Fighting back isn't what Jesus says here. His words are, “…be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.” Shrewd and innocent go together in the same person. A snake's sharpness and a dove's purity, that's the pair.
Synagogues is the word. Jesus says, “…they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues.” He doesn't sugarcoat it. He says it straight.

Markets sound like a busy spot, but Jesus names another place. He says, “…they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues.” The blank wants synagogues. Markets aren't in the verse.
Courtyards don't show up in this verse. Jesus says, “…they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues.” I think this one hurts to hear. The place He names is synagogues.

explanations.answer: Witnesses to them and the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: That's the role Jesus gives. He says, “On My account you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles.” Witnesses are people who speak about what they know. So being brought before governors and kings puts them there as people who speak about Him.

Jesus doesn't describe them as messengers asking for peace. He says they'll be brought before governors and kings “…as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles.” The word is witnesses. That's the job in the room.

Ransom isn't mentioned in this verse. Jesus says they will be brought before governors and kings “On My account…” The role He gives them there is witnesses, people who speak about what they know. That's the one.

explanations.answer: They will be given what to say
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. Jesus says, “…do not worry about how to respond or what to say. In that hour you will be given what to say.” So what to say gets handed to them in that hour. I'd still bring a cookie, but that's just me.
Jesus doesn't promise that. He says, “In that hour you will be given what to say.” The promise is about their words in that moment. Nothing is said about the case being dropped.

explanations.answer: A friend will speak for them
explanations.explanation: A friend isn't what Jesus mentions. He says, “In that hour you will be given what to say.” In the next verse He says, “…it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” So the words come to them in that hour.

Spirit is the word. Jesus says, “For it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” So when the twelve stand up to talk, they aren't doing it on their own. That takes a lot of pressure off the moment.
Jesus doesn't mention an angel here. He says, “…it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” The blank wants Spirit. The speaking happens through the twelve.

A prophet isn't in this verse. Jesus says, “…it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” The word that fits is Spirit. The speaking happens through the twelve, by the Spirit.
True. Jesus says, “You will be hated by everyone because of My name…” This one is heavy, and He says it plainly. The reason in the verse is His name.
It's actually true. Jesus says, “You will be hated by everyone because of My name…” That's a heavy thing to hear, and He doesn't soften it. The next line gives the promise that goes with it.

explanations.answer: The one who perseveres to the end
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. Jesus says, “…the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Persevering means sticking with it all the way. It comes right after He says, “You will be hated by everyone because of My name…”

explanations.answer: The one who stays out of sight
explanations.explanation: Staying out of sight isn't what Jesus says. His words are, “…the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Perseveres is the word. It means sticking with it to the end.

explanations.answer: The one who wins every argument
explanations.explanation: Winning arguments isn't the measure Jesus gives. He says, “…the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” It's about perseverance, not about being right in every debate. Good news for those of us who think of the perfect comeback an hour later.
It's the other way around. Jesus says, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.” So they move on instead of digging in. Leaving is part of His instructions.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.” He doesn't tell them to stand their ground there. They keep moving down the road.

Teacher is the word. Jesus says, “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.” A disciple follows a teacher, and the twelve are His disciples. The line tells them where they stand next to Him.

Student is close in meaning, but it's not the word Jesus uses. He says, “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.” The blank wants teacher. A disciple and a teacher make the pair.
Neighbor doesn't fit this verse. Jesus says, “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.” The comparison is between a disciple and his teacher. That's the pair He uses.

explanations.answer: They will get it even more
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. “If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!” Beelzebul is the name used for the ruler of the demons (Matthew 12:24). So if the head of the house got that name, the household can expect it too.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, “If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!” He's talking about what the household gets called. If the head of the house got that name, the members aren't left alone. They get even more of it.

Praise isn't what Jesus describes. He says, “If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!” He's talking about names, and the head of the house has been called Beelzebul. So the household can expect even more of the same, not praise.
